name: vertical-partitioner-removal
context: The vertical split is designed specifically so a whole field group, subject or segment can be removed independently while everything around it stays intact — a right-to-erasure request against an append-only event store, a retention obligation for one data class, or a tenant offboarding. The mechanics differ from ordinary vertical partitioning: deletion must be provable, must not require rewriting unrelated data, and must be provably propagated to every replica, aggregate and backup that could still re-identify the subject.
benefits: Makes erasure feasible at a granularity that undifferentiated storage cannot offer — the target group is a deletable unit
Destroys data without rewriting history, so immutable audit trails and append-only logs stay intact and verifiable
Key destruction is bit-level final: the ciphertext remains everywhere but becomes permanently unrecoverable, including in replicas and backups
Leaves a tombstone behind so referential integrity survives and an append-only ledger keeps a valid, if dangling, pointer
Allows completeness to be proven from live state rather than asserted — a queryable predicate over key state, orphan counts and preserved facts
tradeoffs: Key-based erasure is only as good as key coverage: any directly identifying column stored in plaintext outside the shredded key survives and re-identifies the subject
Per-subject or per-tenant key separation has a real storage, latency and key-management cost, and the key inventory itself becomes critical infrastructure
Derived stores, search indexes, caches and aggregate rollups are outside the shredded envelope unless they are enumerated explicitly
A wrong key deletion is irreversible and may take out data that retention required you to keep
Undeleting becomes impossible by construction, which conflicts with any requirement to reverse an erroneous erasure
use_cases: GDPR Article 17 erasure against an append-only event store that must keep its audit guarantees
Erasing one tenant from a multi-tenant store without rewriting shared history
Retaining medical or financial identifiers in a separately shreddable group while keeping de-identified aggregates
Destroys a compromised device's credentials and per-device payload group on revocation
Dropping a time range from an append-only time-series store by destroying the segment's key or dropping the chunk
avoid_when: The data is not segmented per subject, per tenant or per field group — without a boundary there is nothing to delete
The obligation permits a retention window and a forward-going delete, which is far cheaper than immediate shredding
Aggregates or rollups already contain the value in a form that cannot be attributed to the subject, and destroying keys will not remove it
The system must be able to undo an erasure, which key destruction makes impossible
component_types: Per-subject key record: stable non-secret reference plus destroyable key material; null key material is the canonical erased state
Tombstone: surviving identifier row that keeps append-only references structurally valid after shredding
Erasable-field group: the vertically split partition whose payload is sealed under the subject key
Purge manifest: explicit enumeration of every plaintext surface that must also be cleared, with per-surface counts captured before the write
Immutability guard: trigger-enforced append-only enforcement on ledgers that must survive the erasure
Completeness predicate: queryable check that the key is destroyed, no enumerated surface retains personal data, and the erasure fact is preserved
technology_stack: Per-subject DEK wrapped by a KEK
AWS KMS / GCP Cloud KMS / Vault Transit
Apache Kafka (null-value tombstones and log compaction)
anti_patterns: Issuing a DELETE against the live table while replicas, backups, search indexes and rollups still hold the subject
Deriving the subject key from a global key-encryption key, which yields revocation, not erasure — the ciphertext remains re-derivable
Shredding without an explicit manifest, so plaintext columns outside the sealed envelope silently survive
Dropping the tombstone row, breaking every append-only record that referenced it
Claiming erasure from the absence of a key with no completeness predicate re-derived from live state
design_principles: Deletability is a design property of the layout, not a runtime operation
Immutable structures survive erasure; the payload becomes unreadable rather than being rewritten
Completeness is provable from live state, not asserted in a ticket
Every surface holding personal data is enumerated; unenumerated surfaces are presumed to survive
Key material is independent of any key that could re-derive it
best_practices: Capture per-surface row counts before the destructive write, since a pointer-only surface counts as data
Perform key shred, plaintext purge and the erasure-fact append in a single transaction so a crash cannot leave a shredded key with un-purged surfaces
Use per-subject keys that are random and independent, not derived from a master key
Keep an append-only erasure ledger recording who, what, when and scope — ids and counts only, never the payload
Test the completeness predicate against a synthetic subject after every schema change that adds a surface
references: halleyhq/crypto-shredder — GDPR-safe erasure for event-sourced systems by per-subject key destruction, https://github.com/halleyhq/crypto-shredder
cqrs-es-crypto, key_store.rs — per-subject DEK management and atomic shredding within a transaction, https://docs.rs/cqrs-es-crypto/latest/src/cqrs_es_crypto/key_store.rs.html
Ink & Switch, Local-first software — local-first data ownership and the tension between immutability and erasure, https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/
Apache Kafka, Core Concepts — KTable null values as delete tombstones and log compaction, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/core-concepts/
TimescaleDB, Hypertables — time-partitioned chunks as independently droppable segments, https://docs.timescale.com/use-timescale/latest/hypertables/
